newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's ancient history inspires name for raid.
newsitem.headline: Peru's ancient history inspires name for raid.

text.p: Military forces went back 3,000 years to find a codename for their spectacularly successful raid on the Japanese ambassador's home, President Alberto Fujimori said on Wednesday.

Operation Chavin de Huantar was the codename they gave Tuesday's raid, in which about 140 army and navy commandos stormed the residence and all but one of the 72 hostages alive after months of top-secret training.
The name recalls ancient ruins in northern Peru that include a network of tunnels and underground passageways -- like the four tunnels through which troops swarmed into the residence.

"This conception is inspired in the archaeological monuments known as Chavin de Huantar," Fujimori told a news conference. "We were inspired by the whole system of underground galleries at Chavin de Huantar."
The ruins in northern Ancash region, built about 2,500 years before the world-famous Machu Picchu citadel, include a large pyramid honeycombed with tunnels and crawlspaces leading to hidden rooms.

The name of the operation was meant as a homage "to the monolithic force of our armed forces and because we used tunnels like in that (ancient) culture," said a military officer who asked not to be identified.

The use of tunnels carries a touch of sweet irony for anti- guerrilla forces, since the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement rebels scored a great propaganda coup via a tunnel in 1990, when 49 of them escaped jail through a secret tunnel.
